That's a fair and honest question, and I want to reassure you: you're not reading anything into the text that isn't already there—you're just noticing that the New Testament makes its case a certain way, and it's worth understanding why. You're right that Jesus doesn't walk around saying "I am God" in those bare words. But think about what he did say and do, and to whom. He said "I AM" absolutely, in a Jewish world where that phrase belonged to YHWH alone. He accepted worship, forgave sins in his own authority, and applied to himself titles Isaiah reserved for the LORD—"every knee should bow" (Philippians 2:10, echoing Isaiah 45:23). These aren't loose compliments; they're deliberate transfers of divine identifiers onto a first-century Galilean, in a culture that would die rather than give God's honors to another (Deuteronomy 6:4; Exodus 20:3-5).

Your real question, though, is sharper: couldn't "Son of God" just mean a lesser, derivative being? Here's the key distinction the book leans on: sonship in this Gospel is about personal relationship and order, not inferiority of nature. When Jesus prays to the Father in John 17, he's not excluding himself from deity—he's asking to be glorified with the glory he had with the Father before the world existed. The Father and Son are really distinct persons, but the text never treats the Son as a diminished kind of God. And notice how the story resolves: the same Gospel that opens "the Word was God" ends with Thomas kneeling before the risen Jesus and confessing, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28)—and Jesus does not correct him. That's not Thomas misunderstanding a Son who is less than God; that's the author telling you what the whole book has been building toward. So it isn't that Jesus never said it plainly—it's that he said it in ways a monotheistic Jew would recognize as claiming the divine Name itself, and let it be confirmed by worship he never refused.
